The test uses the `caplog` fixture to capture vLLM's WARNING logs; however, the vLLM logger is configured with `propagate=False` (in `vllm/logger.py:67`), meaning logs do not propagate to the root logger. Re-compile requirements/test/xpu.txt to update all packages.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][XPU] Fix Mamba state pointer overflow
commits.pr_body:
Fixes #48059

## Purpose

XPU USM device pointers can exceed the positive signed int64 range. The Mamba
align-mode fused copy path stores state tensor and block-table `data_ptr()`
values in `torch.int64` metadata buffers before passing them to Triton kernels,
so assigning a high-bit XPU pointer directly can raise:

```text
ValueError: Overflow when unpacking long long
```

This preserves the 64-bit pointer pattern by reinterpreting unsigned pointer
values as signed int64 before storing them in the existing metadata buffers. The
Triton kernel ABI stays unchanged.

Duplicate-work check: no open PR currently references #48059 or matches the
`state_base_addrs` / overflow keywords.

## Test Plan

commits.pr_title: [CPU] Add AMX-only high-performance MLA backend for DeepSeek V2/V3/R1
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Add `AMXMLABackend`/`AMXMLAImpl`, a high-performance MLA attention backend for
CPU, built on AMX decode/extend/bmm/qkv-proj kernels vendored under
`csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels/`. It plugs into the same `MLACommonBackend`/
`MLACommonImpl` abstraction every other concrete MLA backend uses.

This is a separate, opt-in-by-capability backend alongside the existing
reference `CPUMLABackend` (#49453): that one targets any CPU/dtype at
block_size=16 as a functional/CI reference, not performance. This backend
requires AMX (bf16 only, block_size a multiple of 32) and is preferred
automatically by the platform layer when the host supports it, falling back
to the reference backend otherwise (or when explicitly requested).

## What's included

- Vendored SGLang AMX kernels (`decode.cpp`, `extend.cpp`, `bmm.cpp`,
  `qkv_proj.cpp`) under `csrc/cpu/sgl-kernels/`, AMX-only build-gated.
- `AMXMLABackend`/`AMXMLAImpl` (`vllm/v1/attention/backends/mla/amx_mla.py`):
  weight absorption for prefill via VNNI-packed `W_UK`/`W_UV` computed once at
  load time; `forward_mha` attends directly against the paged latent cache in
  one causal pass (fresh prefill + cached-prefix continuation together, no
  GPU-style decompress-then-dense-attend); `forward_mqa` reuses the existing
  generic decode-side absorption. Per-step-invariant metadata (block-table
  expansion, `req_pool_indices`, `num_kv_splits`, `query_start_loc`
  derivatives) is computed once in `AMXMLAMetadataBuilder.build`, not
  recomputed per layer.
- Platform wiring: `CpuPlatform.get_attn_backend_cls` selects `AMX_MLA` when
  `torch.cpu._is_amx_tile_supported()` and x86 (unless the reference backend
  is explicitly requested); block-size/chunked-prefill config forcing is
  scoped to exclude the AMX path, since the extend kernel handles arbitrary
  prefix length and block size natively.
- Two small, genuine bugs fixed in shared MLA code, both applicable beyond
  this backend: (1) CPU's generic `Linear` weight-packing path was freeing
  `kv_b_proj`'s raw weight before `MLAAttention.process_weights_after_loading`
  could read it to derive `W_UK`/`W_UV`; (2) `get_mla_prefill_backend()`
  unconditionally resolves the CUDA-only `FlashAttnPrefillBackend` when
  `device_capability` is `None`, which asserts at construction time on CPU —
  fixed via a minimal inert CPU prefill backend registration.
- Correctness tests (`tests/kernels/attention/test_amx_mla.py`), gated on
  `torch.cpu._is_amx_tile_supported()`, wired into the x86 CPU CI job.

## Tests

```
pytest -x -v -s tests/kernels/attention/test_amx_mla.py
```
10 passed (stable across repeated runs).

```
pytest -q tests/kernels/attention/test_cpu_attn.py
```
1585 passed, 990 skipped, 0 failed — no regression to the existing dense
`CPU_ATTN` backend from the shared-code changes.

Also verified directly: offline single/multi-prompt inference (coherent,
correct output on `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite`); a forced mixed
decode+prefill batch (confirmed via temporary instrumentation that
`num_decodes>0 and num_prefills>0` in the same step, output unaffected);
tensor parallelism at TP1/TP2/TP4 (correct output, no crashes, expected
sub-linear throughput scaling from cross-socket all-reduce overhead).

## Model evaluation

GSM8K via `lm_eval` (5-shot, full 1319-question test set, `max_model_len=8192`,
`max_gen_toks=512`, TP4, `AMX_MLA` selected):

| Filter | Accuracy | Stderr |
|---|---|---|
| strict-match | 38.44% | ±1.34% |
| flexible-extract | 38.51% | ±1.34% |

Cross-checked against an independent third-party measurement of the same base
model (vllm-ascend's own accuracy report, same `lm_eval` harness):
strict-match 38.13%, flexible-extract 38.36% — within noise of this run.
DeepSeek's own published number for this model is 41.1% (different
harness/shot-count, same ballpark).

`vllm bench serve` (1000 prompts, `random` dataset, 1024in/256out, TP4):
1000/1000 successful, 0 failed, 816.9 tok/s output throughput, 4084.3 tok/s
total. Throughput scaling across TP1→TP2→TP4 (100-question GSM8K): 196.0 →
295.2 → 407.8 tok/s.

commits.pr_title: [XPU] Support EC connector KV Offloading on XPU
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

PR #47423 added `ECCPUConnector` for encoder-cache (EC) offloading to host memory, but the swap path assumed CUDA/ROCm-style raw pointers and was never exercised on XPU. This PR adds XPU support so the EC connector's offload path works correctly on Intel GPUs, and extends CI coverage accordingly.

Three issues were fixed:

### 1. Descriptor pointer dtype on XPU

`swap_blocks_batch` takes `int64` pointer arrays on CUDA/ROCm but `uint64` on XPU, so `DescriptorBufferPool` now selects `_PTR_DTYPE` per platform.

### 2. Pointer assignment overflow

`ECCPUWorker.save_caches` / `start_load_caches` fill those descriptor buffers with raw addresses, and XPU USM pointers have the top bit set (value >= 2\*\*63). Torch range-checks each assigned Python int against the tensor dtype, and **the accepted encoding differs by torch version**: before 2.14 the value is always unpacked as a signed `long long`, while [pytorch#191458](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/191458) (landed as [pytorch@c9f91bd](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/commit/c9f91bddef7d6f2fffced9e9e58d3577af46d34c), released in 2.14) makes the unpacking dtype-aware.

Writing a top-bit pointer into the XPU `uint64` buffer therefore fails on *both* sides depending on how it is encoded:

| assigned value | torch 2.13 (currently pinned) | torch 2.14 |
|---|---|---|
| raw address | ❌ `ValueError: Overflow when unpacking long long` | ✅ |
| two's-complement rewrite (`addr - 2**64`) | ✅ | ❌ `OverflowError: can't convert negative int to unsigned` |

An earlier revision of this PR used the two's-complement rewrite, which crashed the engine on torch 2.14:

```
File "vllm/distributed/ec_transfer/ec_connector/cpu/worker/__init__.py", line 114, in save_caches
    src_ptrs[idx] = encode_ptr_for_dtype(src_base + start, ptr_dtype)
OverflowError: can't convert negative int to unsigned
→ vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError
```

Since vLLM pins `torch==2.13.0` today but must keep working across the 2.14 bump, neither encoding is viable on its own. The descriptor tables are plain CPU tensors, so the pointer arrays are instead filled through **numpy views**, which cast against the array dtype and never go through torch's scalar unpacking — correct on both versions, and already the approach used by the KV-cache offload path (`gpu_worker.py`).

The views are created once per allocation and cached next to the tensors, and the workaround is confined to a single method so it is trivially removable later:

```python
def set_ptrs(self, idx: int, src: int, dst: int) -> None:
    # TODO(torch>=2.14): drop this indirection and assign the tensors
    # directly once the minimum supported torch is 2.14. ...
    self.src_np[idx] = src
    self.dst_np[idx] = dst
```

Only the pointer arrays need this; `sizes` holds byte counts and keeps plain torch assignment.

See [RFC #50834](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50834) for the broader effort to unify device-pointer storage on `torch.uint64`; [this comment](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50834#issuecomment-5312646469) records the version-dependence in detail.

commits.pr_title: [Elastic EP] Reduce eager-mode reconfiguration downtime
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

This PR moves more work out of the blocking commit state to background preparation.

1. Run all preparation steps as one async worker RPC instead of returning to the DP engine core after every step.

2. Create the target EPLB communicator during preparation alongside the other target communicators, then run the post-scale-up EPLB reshuffle asynchronously.

3. During commit, switch to the prepared groups immediately, then destroy the old communication groups in the background, which can take several seconds for large groups.

4. Warm target communication groups during preparation, avoiding the much slower first collective during commit.

This solves eager-mode downtime except for kernel warmup, which will be addressed together with CUDA graph capture in a follow-up PR.

## Results

All tests used NIXL EP, async EPLB, eager execution, warm caches, and one client per DP rank.

`Preparation` is the period during which requests continue to be served unaffected. `Downtime` is the period during which new requests receive HTTP 503 and existing requests are not progressed.

### DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, H100, DP 4 -> 8 -> 4

1 node with 8 * H100 GPUs.

| Direction | Baseline preparation | This PR preparation | Baseline downtime | This PR downtime | Downtime reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Scale up | 32.208 s | 36.723 s | 6.488 s | 1.925 s | 70.3% |
| Scale down | 3.036 s | 4.897 s | 4.227 s | 1.272 s | 69.9% |

### DeepSeek-V3, GB200, DP 16 -> 24 -> 16

6 nodes, 4 GB200 GPUs per node.

| Direction | Baseline preparation | This PR preparation | Baseline downtime | This PR downtime | Downtime reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Scale up | 35.855 s | 42.995 s | 13.172 s | 5.097 s | 61.3% |
| Scale down | 4.108 s | 7.768 s | 7.889 s | 3.264 s | 58.6% |

**The higher downtime in the full-size, multi-node setup comes almost entirely from the longer forward-pass warmup during commit.**

## Follow-up

With these optimizations, we consider eager-mode downtime solved. The next step is to move the max-token warmup and CUDA graph recapture into preparation. For a multi-node DeepSeek-V3 deployment, capture and warmup across the default batch sizes up to 256 take about 37 seconds. This will be addressed in a separate PR.

cc @tlrmchlsmth @SageMoore @ilmarkov

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Elastic EP] Reject scale below the minimum data parallel size
commits.pr_body:
Fixes #30660.

Scaling keeps the per-engine physical expert count fixed, so any target below
`ceil(num_experts * cur_dp / num_physical_experts)` makes `num_redundant_experts`
negative. That request was accepted, then failed on the bare
`assert num_redundant >= 0` in `eplb/policy/default.py`, killing the engine core.

## Test Plan

Qwen3-30B-A3B on 4xH200, launched at DP2:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B --data-parallel-backend ray --data-parallel-size 2 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --enable-expert-parallel --enable-eplb \
  --enable-elastic-ep --api-server-count 1

curl -X POST localhost:8000/scale_elastic_ep -d '{"new_data_parallel_size": 1}'  # below minimum
curl -X POST localhost:8000/scale_elastic_ep -d '{"new_data_parallel_size": 4}'  # legal
```

```bash
pre-commit run --files vllm/v1/engine/core_client.py \
  vllm/entrypoints/serve/elastic_ep/api_router.py
```

## Test Result

Before: `DP2 -> DP1` was accepted, standby groups were created, the reconfiguration
was committed, and then `AssertionError` in `replicate_experts` took down the
engine core; the server was left unusable.

After: `DP2 -> DP1` is rejected with `Cannot scale to data_parallel_size 1, minimum
is 2`, the server stays alive and keeps serving (`/v1/completions` returns 200),
and `DP2 -> DP4` still returns `{"message":"Scaled to 4 data parallel engines"}`.

commits.pr_title: Revert DSv4 eager workspace reuse
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

Revert #49236 and restore allocator-backed temporary buffers in the DeepSeek V4 attention input-preparation path.

This removes the model-wide `DeepseekV4EagerScratchPool`, its output-buffer plumbing, and the out-parameter fused op added by #49236. Later changes on `main` are preserved.

## Why

The model-wide scratch pool can reuse storage across layers and CUDA streams without the caching allocator's stream/event lifetime tracking. That allows a producer to overwrite shared workspace while a previous consumer may still be using it. Reverting restores the pre-#49236 allocation lifetime behavior until safe cross-stream synchronization is implemented.

## Impact

#51430 moved Q projection/KV insertion, indexer preparation, and compressor preparation out of the narrow eager break and into the captured region. The allocator calls restored by this revert are therefore captured on the Model Runner V2 path, so this revert is not expected to give up the 3.9% TTFT improvement originally reported by #49236 there.

#52401 subsequently restored the wide eager region for Model Runner V1 because the narrow region corrupted V1 output. The allocation overhead remains eager on that path, so its TTFT impact is runner-dependent and has not been measured on the current tree.

## Duplicate-work check

This is not duplicating an existing revert. I checked issue #45861 and searched open PRs for references to #49236 and for DeepSeek V4 workspace/eager-scratch reuse. No open PR is dedicated to reverting #49236.

## Validation

- `git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACMR -z | xargs -0 .venv/bin/pre-commit run --files` — passed

commits.pr_title: [Core] Make prefix-cache NONE_HASH deterministic by default
commits.pr_body:
## Summary

Prefix-cache block hashes chain from `NONE_HASH`. When `PYTHONHASHSEED` was unset, `NONE_HASH` was seeded with `os.urandom(32)`, so every process produced different block hashes for identical content. This forced distributed KV cache users (shared-FS/object tiers, Mooncake connector) to pin a common `PYTHONHASHSEED` on every node just to get cache hits, and made the P2P tier refuse to start without it.

This makes `NONE_HASH` derive from a fixed default seed instead, so independent instances share a prefix cache out of the box. `PYTHONHASHSEED`, if set, still overrides the default seed.

Reported by a user who found that all vLLM instances need the same `PYTHONHASHSEED` to reuse KV cache across nodes.

## Why the per-process randomness is no longer needed

The random seed dates to #12621, when prefix caching used Python's built-in `hash()` and a predictable `hash(None)` (constant on Python 3.12+) made intentional collisions feasible. The default hash algorithm is now **SHA-256**, whose collision resistance does not depend on a secret seed, and `cache_salt` is the supported mechanism for intentional cache isolation. The random seed therefore no longer adds meaningful protection while it does add operational complexity.

This also makes CBOR-based hashes reproducible by default, so the prior non-reproducibility warning is removed.

## P2P tier

The P2P tier no longer requires `PYTHONHASHSEED`: it resolves the same effective seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED` or the default) and still advertises and verifies it during the connect handshake, so mismatched peers are rejected loudly instead of silently missing.

## Docs

FS/object tiers, Mooncake connector, and P2P tier docs are updated to reflect that a shared `PYTHONHASHSEED` is now optional.

## Not a duplicate

commits.pr_title: [CI][ROCm] Prevent Git maintenance races during shallow fetches
commits.pr_body:
The ROCm test-image build in [Buildkite build 84415](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/84415/summary?jid=01a015b8-b7d5-453a-9aba-b7ea591fa5a9&tab=output#L86) failed before the Docker build with:

```text
Deepening history to reach a version tag
fatal: shallow file has changed since we read it
```

`ci-bake-rocm.sh` performs several shallow-history fetches in sequence. By default, `git fetch` may start automatic repository maintenance in a detached process. That maintenance can outlive the fetch that launched it and update `.git/shallow` while a later deepen operation is reading it, causing Git's consistency check to abort with exit status 128. The same [Buildkite step was retried on a different agent](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/84415/summary?jid=01a015c3-9b1e-4b7c-b33b-d265fe7aabe6&tab=output) and passed the history-deepening operation, image build, and `AMD image smoke OK`, confirming that the original failure was transient rather than caused by the PR's dependency change. This change:

- adds `--no-auto-maintenance` to the centralized ROCm Git fetch helper;
- applies the protection to both its timeout and no-timeout paths; and
- preserves every fetch caller's existing arguments and failure behavior.

commits.pr_title: [ROCM][CI] Attention test speedup
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Two independent problems make `tests/kernels/attention` far slower than the work it actually performs, and both are addressed here.

**1. `test_merge_attn_states.py` skips its entire matrix on ROCm without reason.**

The test gates all 2592 parametrized cases behind an "only CUDA supports the custom merge_attn_states kernel" check. That is no longer accurate: the kernel source is not CUDA-gated in the build, so it is compiled for ROCm as well, and the op is registered and produces correct results there. The same file already exercises the native kernel on ROCm through its `both_empty` case, which passes today so the wide skip contradicts a test sitting next to it.

The platform check moves from the test body to a module-level condition that accepts CUDA and ROCm. This unlocks 2592 cases of real kernel coverage on ROCm.

Because the check was evaluated inside the test body, every skipped case still paid full setup and teardown, so the group was spending minutes to decide not to test anything.

**2. Pure kernel modules pay a global cleanup after every single test.**

An autouse fixture tears down the distributed environment and empties the allocator caches after each test. The modules touched here do not build an engine and do not initialize distributed state, so there is nothing for that teardown to clean — but it still costs a garbage collection and a cache flush per test, which dominates the group's runtime.

These modules are marked with the existing `skip_global_cleanup` marker, the same mechanism already used at module level elsewhere in the test suite.

Module selection is deliberately conservative. On ROCm the global cleanup also refreshes AITER class-level state that `monkeypatch` does not restore, so every module that touches environment variables or AITER, plus one that patches platform classes, is intentionally left untouched. Nothing is given up by that: the largest modules account for nearly all of the group's runtime.

## Test Plan

Full `tests/kernels/attention` run before and after the change, on a single MI300, same flags and same GPU in both cases. The result was then confirmed a second time with a default environment, to rule out any influence of the flags used while measuring. `test_merge_attn_states.py` was additionally measured on its own, and the unlocked cases were verified independently against the Triton reference path.

## Test Result

Whole group, single MI300:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Wall time | 46:34 | 10:08 |
| Passed | 3207 | 5808 |
| Skipped | 3703 | 1111 |
| Failed | 0 | 0 |

The group is 4.6x faster while running 2601 more tests, with no failures.

`test_merge_attn_states.py` alone goes from 7:23 (6 passed, 2592 skipped) to 0:30 with all 2598 cases passing, fp8 variants included.

All numbers above are from a local MI300. A speedup is expected in CI as well, since the removed per-test cost is not hardware specific, but the magnitude there is not measured here.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][DP] Don't assume the engines started when forwarding a wake
commits.pr_body:
Fixes the first of the two problems described in #51476.

## Purpose

`DPCoordinator` holds `engines_running`. Front-ends read it through `dp_engines_running()`, and `wait_for_requests_to_drain()` polls it. It is written in two places, and the two writes are not the same kind of claim:

- **True** is set when the coordinator *forwards* a wake — `FIRST_REQ` → broadcast `START_DP_WAVE` ([coordinator.py:361](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/engine/coordinator.py#L361)). Nothing is confirmed; the coordinator assumes the engines will act on the broadcast.
- **False** is set when DP rank 0 reports `wave_complete`, having observed the group go idle.

True is a prediction. False is an observation.

The two-phase pause added `ignore_start_dp_wave`: once the ranks reach pause consensus, **every rank discards `START_DP_WAVE`** ([core.py:2054](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/engine/core.py#L2054)). That removes the premise the prediction rests on. A request arriving after `pause_generation(mode="abort")` makes the coordinator set True, no engine steps, no `wave_complete` is ever produced, and the flag stays True for the life of the process.

The state is unrecoverable: aborting the request does not help, because nothing makes a paused engine step. `wait_for_requests_to_drain()` can then only end in a `TimeoutError`, and the stale True is published to every front-end, where `add_request_async` skips `FIRST_REQ` because it believes the engines are already running.

This is not pause-specific: any mechanism that stops engines from stepping reaches the same state. A request arriving while the engines are `sleep()`ing latches the flag identically, which the second of the two new tests pins down. `_drain_requests_for_elastic_ep` is the only in-tree caller of `wait_for_requests_to_drain`, so that scaling path takes its go/no-go from the same signal.

## Change

Stop predicting. Report both edges from where they happen.

- `coordinator.py`: the `FIRST_REQ` branch still broadcasts, but no longer claims the result.
- `core.py`: rank 0 already reports the True→False edge as `wave_complete`. It now reports False→True from the same place, as the `elif` of that branch, reusing the existing `start_wave` field that the coordinator already interprets as "engines started" ([coordinator.py:436](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/engine/coordinator.py#L436)).

The report sits after `self.engines_running = self._has_global_unfinished_reqs(...)`, which is where the engine that received the request actually transitions — an equal-wave `ADD` does not set the flag in `add_request`. Reporting from the top of the busy loop instead reads the previous iteration's value and misses the edge entirely; the first assertion in the pause test exists to catch exactly that.

Three guards on the new branch: `not was_running` makes it an edge rather than a per-iteration message; `dp_rank == 0` keeps a single writer, matching the existing `wave_complete` convention; `not pending_pause` excludes the kick-start in phase 1 of the pause protocol, which sets `engines_running = True` only so that an idle rank stops `continue`-ing and reaches the consensus all-reduce.

No new message type, no new field, no new socket, and no notion of pausing inside the coordinator. Its `engines_running` becomes rank 0's `engines_running`, one message behind: a single writer, both edges from one source.

### Not #38009

[#38009](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/38009) was rejected for adding per-engine state that diverged across ranks and deadlocked an all-reduce. Here the decision stays in the single coordinator process. The engine side gains one `output_queue.put_nowait` — a report, not a decision — emitted by rank 0 only, after the existing collective has completed. `was_running` is a per-iteration local snapshot: it does not change any rank's participation in any collective, nor any input to `sync_dp_state()`.

### Cost

The coordinator now lags engine start by one round trip (broadcast → step → report). Walking every reader of the flag:

| path | which copy it reads | effect |
|---|---|---|
| offline `LLMEngine` (`SyncMPClient`) | its own local copy — `add_request` sets True, `wave_complete` sets False | none; coordinator publishes never reach it |
| SPMD / no coordinator | — | none; the new report is gated on `has_coordinator` |
| elastic-EP state sync (`elastic_state.py`) | the engine's own `engines_running` | none |
| online API server (`DPAsyncMPClient`) | the coordinator's 100ms publish | a second `FIRST_REQ` can be sent inside the lag window, costing one extra broadcast; engines are idempotent there, so it never causes an extra step |
| `wait_for_requests_to_drain` | same | can return one round trip early |

Measured on 2-way DP + EP with the coordinator instrumented, over four wave starts: **4 `START_DP_WAVE` broadcasts unpatched, 7 patched**, with rank 0 emitting exactly one `start_wave` report per wave start. The extra broadcast is the coordinator's own echo when it processes the report. A burst of 16 concurrent requests produced **one** broadcast in both arms — the client-side `FIRST_REQ` throttle is untouched.

The early return trades a false positive that hangs for 300s and cannot recover for a false negative of a few milliseconds, and downstream operations carry their own barrier (`sleep()` contains the pause consensus). That window is not removable in this architecture: an engine that is not stepping cannot report, so any scheme that waits for an acknowledgement re-latches under pause.

## Test Plan

Two tests in `tests/v1/distributed/test_async_llm_dp.py`, MoE-only because `enable_wave_coordination` is `model_config.is_moe`, so a dense model never reaches this coordinator state.

`test_dp_pause_late_request_does_not_block_drain` has to rule out two different failures, since a signal that is never True satisfies every drain assertion while being useless. It asserts, in order:

1. the engines report themselves as running two seconds into a live request — past the coordinator's 100ms publishes, so the front-end's own optimistic value has been overwritten by then;
2. the flag returns to False when that request finishes;
3. after `pause(mode="abort")` and a late request, the flag first goes True (the latch is armed — otherwise the next assertion is vacuous) and then settles back to False by itself;
4. the late request was held rather than dropped, and completes on resume.

`test_dp_sleep_late_request_does_not_block_drain` pins the same latch reached through `sleep()`, with the same arm-then-settle structure, and checks the held request survives `wake_up()`. It is worth guarding separately because it is the shape that reaches `_drain_requests_for_elastic_ep`.

## Test Result

All runs on `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` (`0.26.1rc1.dev457+gc810e5ee9`) with this diff applied to the image's `site-packages`, each arm printing which variant it loaded. `before` is the unpatched image; `after` is the same image with this change.

| suite | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `test_async_llm_dp.py -k "dp_pause or dp_sleep"` | **2 failed** / 8 passed | **10 passed** |
| `test_engine_core_client.py` (4 GPUs, full file) | 22 passed | 22 passed |
| `test_pp_dp_v2.py` (DP=2, PP=2, MoE) | 6 passed | 6 passed |
| `test_internal_lb_dp.py` (1 and 4 API servers) | 10 passed | 10 passed |

The two `before` failures are exactly the two new tests, each failing on the assertion that the flag settles back to False. Every pre-existing case passes in both arms, including `test_dp_pause_keep_race_staggered_engines` and `test_dp_pause_barrier_request_deadlock`, the all-reduce rendezvous guards. The full `test_async_llm_dp.py` file, with ray installed, is 23 passed / 4 skipped in the `after` arm.

Beyond the suites, on 2-way DP + EP:

- **Scenarios.** A live request must report True; it must return to False when idle; a late request after `pause(abort)` must settle back; a request admitted microseconds before the pause lands must not strand drain; a request arriving while `sleep()`ing must not latch and must complete on `wake_up()`. All pass. The pause and sleep cases latch on unpatched code — polling for 30s after the late request never observes False, in either flavour. The instrumented coordinator log shows every True paired with a later `wave_complete`, and no True at all while paused or asleep.
- **Stress.** 20 rounds alternating `abort`/`keep`/`wait`, varying in-flight request count and how long before the pause lands: 0 hangs, every request completed, identical to baseline.

## Essential Elements

- Not a duplicate: no open PR matches `engines_running`, `DPCoordinator drain`, or `pause coordinator`. Filed as part of #51476.
- Control-plane only; no effect on model output, so no eval run is included.
- AI assistance was used. The submitter has reviewed each changed line and the runs above.

## Purpose

  `ModelConfig.is_hybrid`'s carve-out for granite-4.0-micro (a hybrid-capable architecture with zero actual mamba layers) only matched `layer_types` entries spelled `"attention"`. Transformers >= 5.13 normalizes pure-attention entries to `"full_attention"` instead (the model's own

  As a result `is_hybrid` stayed `True` for granite-4.0-micro. Combined with prefix caching now defaulting `mamba_cache_mode` to `"align"` for any hybrid-flagged model, `_get_mamba_bufs()` runs unconditionally and hits `AssertionError: no mamba layers in the model` on the first
  inference request — the engine starts and loads fine, then dies on the first completion.

  Fix: match both spellings in the carve-out.

  AI assistance was used to root-cause and author this fix; I reviewed every changed line and reproduced/verified the behavior end-to-end myself before opening this PR.

  ## Test Plan

  Reproduced on vLLM HEAD `37c3bdf5a` (2026-08-13):
```
  vllm serve ibm-granite/granite-4.0-micro --max-model-len 8192
  # then, once the server is up:
  curl http://localhost:8000/v1/completions \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"model":"ibm-granite/granite-4.0-micro","prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":10}'
```

  Then applied the fix and repeated the same two steps, plus a direct property check:
```python
  from vllm.config import ModelConfig
  mc = ModelConfig(model="ibm-granite/granite-4.0-micro")
  print(mc.is_hybrid)
```

  **Before fix:** server starts and loads the model successfully, then the completion request fails the engine:

```
    File ".../vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py", line 4437, in execute_model
      mamba_bufs = self._get_mamba_bufs()
    File ".../vllm/v1/worker/mamba_utils.py", line 554, in get_mamba_groups
```

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][MLA] Do not use Dense MHA for GLM-5.2
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Fix incorrect short-prefill dispatch in the NVIDIA DeepSeek-V3.2 attention
wrapper.

The generic sparse-MLA metadata path may select dense MHA when a prefill's
sequence length is at most `index_topk`. It then allows the sparse indexer to
skip top-k scoring. `DeepseekV32Attention`, however, only invokes
`forward_mqa`; it does not execute the dense-MHA backend. For a pure prefill
above the backend's decode-like threshold, MQA therefore consumed the cleared
all-`-1` top-k buffer and GLM-5.2 output degenerated into repeated tokens.

This change adds a model-layer dense-prefill capability in addition to the
backend capability. The NVIDIA DeepSeek-V3.2 wrapper declares that it is
MQA-only, so sparse MLA keeps its prefill on top-k MQA and the indexer does not
advertise the dense-MHA scoring skip.

This does not duplicate the open related work:

- #51395 disables dense prefill only for the SM120 sparse-MLA backend.
- #52046 adds a dense branch for the PCP path; the reproduced failure is the
  non-PCP SM100 path.
- #49790 routes DSA architectures to the NVIDIA implementation but does not
  resolve this dispatch mismatch.

Issue #46715 reports a different GLM-5.1 failure at a 65,536-token scheduler
budget and multi-thousand-token prompts on the registered model path.

## Test Plan

```text
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py -q

pre-commit run --files \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py \
  vllm/models/deepseek_v32/attention.py \
  tests/model_executor/layers/test_mla_short_prefill_indexer.py
```

Real-model validation uses `nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4`, TP=4, the explicit NVIDIA
DeepSeek-V3.2 class override, FP8 E4M3 KV cache, eager execution, FP32 indexer
logits, GVR disabled, and FlashInfer autotuning disabled. It serially probes
the 128/129-token routing boundary without setting
`sparse_mla_force_mqa=true`.

## Test Result

- Focused pytest: `7 passed`.
- Pre-commit on all three changed files: all hooks passed.
- `compileall` and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Before this change, the real model passed through 127 actual prompt tokens
  and failed at 129 and every tested larger prompt through 1,001 tokens. Adding
  only `sparse_mla_force_mqa=true` made all 19 boundary cases pass, causally
  confirming the routing mismatch.
- Patched real-model result: all 19/19 cases passed exact retrieval without the
  force-MQA workaround, spanning 97, 101, 122, 127, 129, 130, 131, 132, 162,
  191, 192, 193, 194, 196, 202, 257, 301, 502, and 1,001 actual prompt tokens.

AI assistance was used to diagnose, implement, test, and draft this change.
The human submitter must review every changed line and understand and defend
the change end-to-end before marking the PR ready for review.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Perf] Enable fused KDA decode on gfx942 (MI325X)
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

PR #50654 added the fused Kimi-K3 KDA decode kernel (`csrc/libtorch_stable/kimi_k3/fused_kda_decode_kernel_rocm.cu`), but gated it to gfx950 (MI355X) in two places, so it never activates on gfx942 (MI325X):

- **Build gate** — `CMakeLists.txt` filtered the HIP source to `gfx950` only, so the kernel was not compiled and `VLLM_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_DECODE` (and therefore `torch.ops._C.fused_kda_decode`) was never defined on a gfx942-only build.
- **Runtime gate** — `is_fused_kda_decode_supported()` in `vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_decode.py` ended with `return on_gfx950()`.

This change extends both gates to gfx942 as well, so MI325X can take the fused decode path instead of falling back to the three-launch Triton path.

The kernel body is unchanged. It uses only CDNA-common primitives — wave64, DPP row/quad permutes (`quad_perm`, `row_half_mirror`, `row_mirror`), `__builtin_nontemporal_load/store`, and bf16 intrinsics — with no MFMA / FP8 / gfx950-only paths, so no source-level changes are required for gfx942. LDS use is ~2.8 KiB/block and register pressure ~130 VGPR, both well within CDNA3 limits.

## Changes

- `CMakeLists.txt`: HIP arch filter `gfx950` -> `gfx942|gfx950` (and comment).
- `vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_decode.py`: gate `on_gfx950()` -> `on_gfx950() or on_gfx942()`.
- `tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_kda_decode.py`: extend the module skip guard from gfx950 to gfx942 / gfx950 so the correctness suite runs on MI325X.

All other backends and the CUDA path are unchanged; the shape/dtype/head-count guards in `is_fused_kda_decode_supported()` are unchanged.

## Performance

The kernel-level win is large, but the end-to-end win on MI325X is currently small: the Kimi-K3 decode step is dominated by the MXFP4 MoE (int4) and the MLA attention plus the TP8 collectives, which dwarf the KDA linear-attention block. The fusion removes ~66 us of per-layer kernel time (mostly launch overhead), but that is a small fraction of today's total per-token cost. It should become more visible once #50817 (MXFP4 MoE Triton a16w4 for gfx942) lands and shrinks the dominant MoE cost — the fixed KDA saving then represents a larger share of a smaller decode step.

### End-to-end (tp8, 256-in / 256-out, max-concurrency 4)

| Metric | Triton fallback | Fused KDA | Delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mean TPOT (ms) | 425.95 | 422.66 | -0.77% |
| P99 TPOT (ms) | 427.64 | 424.19 | -0.81% |
| Output tok/s | 9.29 | 9.36 | +0.75% |
| Mean TTFT (ms) | 1577.24 | 1574.03 | -0.20% (flat) |

TTFT is unchanged, as expected for a decode-only kernel.

### Per-layer kernel sequence (torch profiler medians, us)

Baseline runs the KDA decode as ~16 separate kernels per layer — the conv1d update, the recurrent delta-rule step, and the gated output RMSNorm decomposed into a chain of launch-overhead-bound (~4 us floor) elementwise ops. Fused collapses all of them into a single kernel:

| # | Baseline kernel | us | Fused kernel | us |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | _causal_conv1d_update_kernel | 5.01 | kda_decode_fusion_kernel<true, 12, true, true, true> | 7.77 |
| 2 | fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode_kernel | 6.45 | | |
| 3 | __amd_rocclr_copyBuffer | 4.37 | | |
| 4 | bfloat16->float32 copy | 4.41 | | |
| 5 | pow (tensor, scalar) | 4.41 | | |
| 6 | reduce Mean | 5.01 | | |
| 7 | add | 4.45 | | |
| 8 | rsqrt | 4.37 | | |
| 9 | mul | 4.21 | | |
| 10 | bfloat16->float32 copy | 4.17 | | |
| 11 | mul | 4.21 | | |
| 12 | bfloat16->float32 copy | 4.45 | | |
| 13 | sigmoid | 5.05 | | |
| 14 | mul | 4.33 | | |
| 15 | float32->bfloat16 copy | 4.49 | | |
| 16 | __amd_rocclr_copyBuffer | 4.57 | | |
| | **total (16 kernels)** | **~73.96** | **total (1 kernel)** | **7.77** |

~9.5x less kernel time for the KDA decode block (~74 -> 7.8 us/layer). The `12` template arg is 12 heads/rank (96 KDA heads at TP8). Across the model's KDA layers (~69 per the kernel header) that is ~4.6 ms/token of raw kernel time removed, in the same ballpark as the ~3.3 ms/token TPOT drop measured above (the remainder overlaps with other work).

## Not a duplicate


- `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "KDA decode gfx942"`
- `gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "fused_kda_decode MI325"`

## Test Plan

Run on an MI325X (gfx942) box after building with gfx942 in the arch list:

1. Build compiles the kernel and registers the op: `python -c "import torch, vllm; print(hasattr(torch.ops._C, 'fused_kda_decode'))"` -> expect `True`.
2. Kernel correctness: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/models/kimi_k3/test_amd_kda_decode.py -v`
3. Model accuracy (output-affecting change) — serve Kimi-K3 on MI325X and run gsm8k, compared against the Triton fallback path: `make gsm8k`
4. Decode latency / throughput before vs after (fused vs Triton fallback): `make bench-kda-mi325`

## Test Result


- Op registered: **True** on the gfx942 build (`hasattr(torch.ops._C, "fused_kda_decode")`); the fused kernel appears in the trace (see Performance).
- Latency/throughput: **-0.77% mean TPOT**, +0.75% output tok/s
- gsm8k (fused vs Triton): **parity** — both 1.00 exact_match on flexible-extract and strict-match (5-shot, limit=100, stderr 0). The fused kernel matches the Triton fallback exactly.
- `test_amd_kda_decode.py`: **12/12 passed** on MI325X (gfx942) — fused output matches the Triton reference across heads {12, 24, 96} x tokens {1, 7, 128}, plus the null-slot, no-output-norm, and padding edge cases.

## Checklist

- [x] Compiles for gfx942 (kernel present in the .so with gfx942 codegen)
- [x] `test_amd_kda_decode.py` passes on MI325X (12/12)
- [x] gsm8k parity with the Triton path
- [x] AI assistance used (see below)

## AI assistance

This change was drafted with AI assistance (Claude). A human must review every line and run the build, tests, and eval on MI325X hardware before merge; the correctness and accuracy results above are not yet filled in.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm] Gate Torch FP8 scaled-MM on architecture support
commits.pr_body:
## Purpose

Reject Torch FP8 scaled-MM kernels when the underlying PyTorch operator is unavailable.

The existing implementation compares a CUDA-style numeric capability against the SM89 threshold. On ROCm, gfx1100 reports capability `110`, so it incorrectly passes this check even though RDNA3 has no native FP8 matrix support and `torch._scaled_mm` rejects the device at runtime.

This change mirrors PyTorch’s current ROCm architecture gate for per-tensor, channel-wise, and row-wise Torch FP8 kernels while preserving existing CPU, CUDA, and XPU behavior. It does not change general FP8 support for Triton, upcast, or emulation paths.

This does not duplicate #43615: that PR enables RDNA4 paths but does not fix the inherited per-tensor/channel-wise eligibility check on gfx1100.

Once `torch.cuda.is_scaled_mm_supported()` is available in vLLM’s supported PyTorch baseline, the mirrored architecture gate can be replaced with that query.

AI assistance was used; all changed lines were reviewed by the submitter.

## Test Plan

```bash
ruff check vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/pytorch.py
ruff format --check vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/pytorch.py

HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python /tmp/validate_vllm_fp8_scaled_mm.py
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 python /tmp/validate_vllm_fp8_scaled_mm.py
```

The standalone script validates:

- CPU, XPU, CUDA, and ROCm routing behavior.
- gfx1100 rejects all three Torch FP8 scaled-MM variants.
- gfx1201 accepts all three variants.
- The underlying PyTorch operator rejects gfx1100.
- Tensor-wise and row-wise execution succeeds on gfx1201 and matches an FP32 reference.

## Test Result

- Ruff passed.

```text
relative_error=0.001601
```

The local vLLM extensions were ABI-incompatible with the installed PyTorch, so validation covered vLLM’s Python selection logic and the underlying PyTorch operator directly rather than a full end-to-end model serving run.

commits.pr_title: [MOE] Standardize and abstract fused shared expert optimization selection
commits.pr_body:
## Disclosure

AI assistance was used. The changes were reviewed and tested manually.

## Purpose

Standardize fused shared-expert (FSE) detection so model construction and checkpoint loading use the same quantization-compatible decision **throughout all models implementing FSE**.

This is e.g. useful for:

- `shared_expert` fusion through arbitrary quantization methods/config (e.g. later on with online quantization in https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51285 / https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51392), so that FSE compatibility can be detected more largely based on arbitrary quantization config across all model archs, and not simply based on logic specific to e.g. [qwen3/quark](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fac808b36f502d0d992509a187dca94c68b0360a/vllm/model_executor/models/qwen3_next.py#L81-L98 )

The shared resolver validates FSE against the quantization configuration, rejects an incompatible requested FSE configuration, and ensures all MoE layers in a model agree on the resolved state. The mixed-state error reports the counts of enabled and disabled layers.

Behavior change compared with `main`:

- Models with mixed resolved FSE states now raise `NotImplementedError`. FSE is only supported/tested for all (or none) layers currently, within a PP rank.
